Ever wanted a pure-TeX implementation of the Lean kernel? No? Oh... Well, I made you one anyway.

kernel.tex

Please see https://github.com/kim-em/overfull for instructions for running it, and https://arena.lean-lang.org/checker/overfull/ for its performance on the Lean Kernel Arena. It is nowhere close to checking all of Mathlib, but it actually does quite a bit better on the kernel arena if you give it longer time limits.

Don't ask too closely about its provenance: I fed lean4lean into the maw of the shoggoths. I am looking forward to this announcement provoking more performant and/or obfuscated esolang implementations in the near future.

(Also for your enjoyment, a Fortan port of nanoclo, and a Cobol port of lean4lean, both passing all the kernel arena tests. Both check Mathlib, but the Cobol port is slightly too slow for the Kernel Arena.)
So now TeX, Fortran, and Cobol are esolangs? Piet and Befunge are offended.
More seriously, I think a Forth implementation could be wild
Can I request a version for Babbage’s analytical engine?
I want an explicit single tape Turing machine version

Since you are making kernels in wierd languages, any interest in making one in Cake ML with a HOL verification. Maybe also one in pure byte code, with an MM0 proof of correctness in PA. (Both just for fun of course :smile:.)

Jason Rute said:

Since you are making kernels in wierd languages, any interest in making one in Cake ML with a HOL verification. Maybe also one in pure byte code, with an MM0 proof of correctness in PA. (Both just for fun of course :smile:.)

I am letting my Codex write a Lean checker based on con-leche which should produce a proof in my own system, which is logically very close to MM0 & set theory with 999999999999 universes. That should be not too different from creating a MM0 proof. (on the other hand, it is quite struggling so far -- working for 1 day, 34k LOC).

I know this is different from MM-C proven specification. On the other hand, MM-C's logic is not strong enough to cover the universes, so ideally there should be a combination in MM0 which can use both set theory with extra universes to prove correctness, and can verify machine code.

Leo advertised the COBOL and Fortran kernels on X today. I’m still missing the point. Is the idea that these langauages (and Tex) are so different from Rust/Lean/etc that they would catch any compiler bugs? Can they handle the bugnum needs of Lean? Can they check practical stuff like Navier Stokes?

They are poking fun at people who think we need more kernels. :woman_shrugging: (Plus a bit of "haha, you can do such ridiculous things with minimal effort with modern AI".) Honestly, that really was my motivation. I spent about an hour on the Tex+Fortran+Cobol kernels on a Sunday afternoon.

In a rare moment of agreement with Patrick Massot, I am personally not that excited about soundness bugs. I think we've got them all fixed now, and the absolute correctness guarantee of Lean has never particularly motivated me. I want to do research, discover new maths, build new algorithms, rewrite software to be safer and faster, etc. etc. Lean is amazing for all of these things, and it being roughly as correct as it has been (indeed, a fair bit more broken would be fine too!) is plenty.

It's good of course to stay out ahead of soundness bugs, I wish we hadn't had that "in the wild" proof of False, and I'm very happy to put in effort to help there. But ... it's just not the point.

I don't object to people taking a TeX port of a Lean kernel seriously if they want to, but that was not my intention.
This is some serious mad scientist stuff, tip of the hat.

FWIW, I agree the independent kernel thing is a bit misguided. (Especially since no one is going to run all these kernels on their project.) I think con leche and kernel verification is a much better direction (that, and serious, sober thought about what is the TCB of Lean). (As for if this matters in practice, it depends on the use case. Lean is a lot of different things to a lot of people.)

Kim Morrison said:

Lean is amazing for all of these things, and it being roughly as correct as it has been (indeed, a fair bit more broken would be fine too!) is plenty.

It's good of course to stay out ahead of soundness bugs, I wish we hadn't had that "in the wild" proof of False, and I'm very happy to put in effort to help there. But ... it's just not the point.

I do agree with this from a research perspective of primarily human-written Lean. Plenty of more experimental proof assistants even take type-in-type or other unsound extensions because the interest is less so adversarial correctness versus research directions. Another part where I do agree with you is that I'm not convinced of the value of adding additional kernels. My reason is perhaps different: I personally agree with the type theorists whose view is that so long as Lean's implementation remains an under-approximation of an undecidable type theory that the value of additional kernels is questionable. (The nuance of checkers that do include a modelling aspect like con-leche is interesting here though.)

But if you take as a given that "Lean's minimal trusted kernel guarantees absolute correctness" is meant to hold in the context of AI-written Lean, I think it is necessary that kernel verification and soundness are focal points. We have well-informed folks taking bets about the chance of major AI-written Lean developments exploiting kernel bugs. It seems like a very legitimate concern to me.

Sure, legitimate, just fairly minor compared to everything else going on at the moment. e.g. I think Marc's new lean formatter probably has higher value for the community than any further kernels or specification work. :woman_shrugging:

I don't mean to discount the autoformatter work at all, I agree this is very high value! For better or worse though, there is a good deal of employment, funding, and publicity tied to using Lean in an adversarial context. So I see soundness and kernel verification as having serious second-order effects on even members of the community that don't use AI at all. Not that this is being ignored completely, I think for instance that lean4#14977 is a great step in the right direction that seems to have gotten some positive reception.

Kim Morrison said:

"haha, you can do such ridiculous things with minimal effort with modern AI".

In such cases, the effort is kind of the point. You don't need to minimize it.

Kim Morrison said:

I am looking forward to this announcement provoking more performant and/or obfuscated esolang implementations in the near future.

I just hope that this will be the result of people spending their evenings tinkering and being proud of the outcome, rather than of a few thoughtless AI prompts.
